items.readable_text:
Content:
We can combine vertical and horizontal shifts and stretches to get new transformed secant and cosecant curves. For example, let's draw the graph of the curve
[MATH: y = 2 \sec\left(x- \dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) + 1.]

Content:
To plot the given curve, we follow these steps:

Content:
- Start with the graph of [MATH: y=\sec{x}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ec9b2015645b95348d99d8e9941661ba]

Content:
- Then, stretch it parallel to the [MATH: y]-axis by a stretch factor of [MATH: 2] to give [MATH: y=2\sec{x}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/33f3f0e47172000728c81f072ae0e780]

Content:
- Next, shift to the right by [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{8}] units to give [MATH: y=2\sec\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{8}\right).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/00ceda514df4f31d3d5a827b5d40f3b9]

Content:
- Finally, shift it up by [MATH: 1] unit to give [MATH: y=2\sec\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) + 1.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4a82346b110fb600bb6d9336222e2c69]

items.title: Identifying the Vertical Shift of a Transformed Secant or Cosecant Curve

sections.normalized_html: The graph below shows the function [MATH: y=\csc{\left(2x\right)}+D,] where [MATH: D] is a constant. What is the value of [MATH: D?]
sections.readable_text:
The graph below shows the function [MATH: y=\csc{\left(2x\right)}+D,] where [MATH: D] is a constant. What is the value of [MATH: D?]

[IMG: /graphics/933477a9e82e9ce55df6624d5d3f7581]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The constant [MATH: D] represents a vertical shift of the function [MATH: y=\csc\left(2x\right).]

Since the local minimum of cosecant is [MATH: y=1,] from the graph we see that the given curve is shifted down by [MATH: 1] unit. So, the equation of the curve is

[MATH: y=\csc\left(2x\right)-1.]

Therefore, [MATH: D =-1.]

sections.normalized_html: The graph above shows a section of the function [MATH: y=\csc{\left(Bx-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)},] where [MATH: B] is a constant. What is the value of [MATH: B?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/d4215af119e817864f364427ce8c3381]

The graph above shows a section of the function [MATH: y=\csc{\left(Bx-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)},] where [MATH: B] is a constant. What is the value of [MATH: B?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The period of the function is

[MATH: T = \frac{27\pi}{4} -\frac{3\pi}{4} = \frac{24\pi}{4} = 6\pi.]

The formula for the period of the function [MATH: y=A\csc(Bx + C) + D] is given by

[MATH: T = \dfrac{2\pi}{B}.]

Applying the formula for [MATH: T] gives

[MATH: 6\pi = \dfrac{2\pi}{B} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad B = \dfrac{2\pi}{6\pi} = \dfrac 1 3.]

So [MATH: B=\dfrac 1 3,] and therefore, the equation of the function is

[MATH: y=\csc\left(\dfrac x 3-\dfrac\pi 4\right).]

items.title: Identifying the Horizontal Stretch and Vertical Shift of a Transformed Secant or Cosecant Curve

sections.normalized_html: The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=\sec{(Bx)}+D,] where [MATH: B] and [MATH: D] are constants. What is [MATH: B+D?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/8b8bf5f8b27be8a4a42104790c0e1ad6]

The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=\sec{(Bx)}+D,] where [MATH: B] and [MATH: D] are constants. What is [MATH: B+D?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The period of the function is [MATH: T = \dfrac{3\pi}4 - \left(-\dfrac \pi 4\right) = \pi.]

The formula for the period of the function [MATH: y=A\sec(Bx + C) + D] is given by

[MATH: T = \dfrac{2\pi}{B}.]

Applying the formula of the period, we get

[MATH: \pi = \dfrac{2\pi}{B}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad B = \dfrac{2\pi}{\pi} = 2.]

The parameter [MATH: D] represents the vertical shift of the secant function. Since the local minimum of secant is [MATH: y=1,] we see that the function has been translated by [MATH: 2] units up. Therefore, [MATH: D=2.]

So, we have [MATH: B+D = 2+2 = 4.]

Finally, the equation of the curve is

[MATH: y=\sec\left(2x\right)+2.]

items.title: Identifying the Horizontal Shift of a Horizontally Stretched Secant or Cosecant Curve

sections.normalized_html: The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=\sec{\left(2x+C\right)},] where [MATH: C] is a constant. Given that [MATH: -\pi < C < \pi,] what is the value of [MATH: C?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/b9701f3385d0607674c049539ef38542]

The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=\sec{\left(2x+C\right)},] where [MATH: C] is a constant. Given that [MATH: -\pi < C < \pi,] what is the value of [MATH: C?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The parameter [MATH: C] represents a horizontal shift of the function.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring out the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

[MATH: y|= \sec (2x + C); = \sec (2(x + (C)/(2)))]

From the graph, we see that the graph of secant has been shifted by [MATH: \dfrac 1 2] units to the left. Therefore,

[MATH: \dfrac C 2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C = 1.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can combine vertical and horizontal shifts and stretches to get new transformed secant and cosecant curves. For example, let's draw the graph of the curve
[MATH: y = 2 \sec\left(x- \dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) + 1.]

Content:
To plot the given curve, we follow these steps:

Content:
- Start with the graph of [MATH: y=\sec{x}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ec9b2015645b95348d99d8e9941661ba]

Content:
- Then, stretch it parallel to the [MATH: y]-axis by a stretch factor of [MATH: 2] to give [MATH: y=2\sec{x}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/33f3f0e47172000728c81f072ae0e780]

Content:
- Next, shift to the right by [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{8}] units to give [MATH: y=2\sec\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{8}\right).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/00ceda514df4f31d3d5a827b5d40f3b9]

Content:
- Finally, shift it up by [MATH: 1] unit to give [MATH: y=2\sec\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) + 1.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4a82346b110fb600bb6d9336222e2c69]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying the Vertical Shift of a Transformed Secant or Cosecant Curve

Example Prompt:
The graph below shows the function [MATH: y=\csc{\left(2x\right)}+D,] where [MATH: D] is a constant. What is the value of [MATH: D?]

[IMG: /graphics/933477a9e82e9ce55df6624d5d3f7581]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The constant [MATH: D] represents a vertical shift of the function [MATH: y=\csc\left(2x\right).]

Since the local minimum of cosecant is [MATH: y=1,] from the graph we see that the given curve is shifted down by [MATH: 1] unit. So, the equation of the curve is

[MATH: y=\csc\left(2x\right)-1.]

Therefore, [MATH: D =-1.]

The constant [MATH: C] represents a horizontal shift of the function [MATH: y=\dfrac 1 2\sec x.]

[MATH: y=\dfrac 1 2\sec\left(x-1\right).]

Item 8 — Example: Identifying the Horizontal Stretch of a Transformed Secant or Cosecant Curve

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/d4215af119e817864f364427ce8c3381]

The graph above shows a section of the function [MATH: y=\csc{\left(Bx-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)},] where [MATH: B] is a constant. What is the value of [MATH: B?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The period of the function is

[MATH: T = \frac{27\pi}{4} -\frac{3\pi}{4} = \frac{24\pi}{4} = 6\pi.]

The formula for the period of the function [MATH: y=A\csc(Bx + C) + D] is given by

[MATH: T = \dfrac{2\pi}{B}.]

Applying the formula for [MATH: T] gives

[MATH: 6\pi = \dfrac{2\pi}{B} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad B = \dfrac{2\pi}{6\pi} = \dfrac 1 3.]

So [MATH: B=\dfrac 1 3,] and therefore, the equation of the function is

[MATH: y=\csc\left(\dfrac x 3-\dfrac\pi 4\right).]

Item 11 — Example: Identifying the Horizontal Stretch and Vertical Shift of a Transformed Secant or Cosecant Curve

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/8b8bf5f8b27be8a4a42104790c0e1ad6]

The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=\sec{(Bx)}+D,] where [MATH: B] and [MATH: D] are constants. What is [MATH: B+D?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The period of the function is
[MATH: T = \dfrac{3\pi}4 - \left(-\dfrac \pi 4\right) = \pi.]

The formula for the period of the function [MATH: y=A\sec(Bx + C) + D] is given by

[MATH: T = \dfrac{2\pi}{B}.]

Applying the formula of the period, we get

[MATH: \pi = \dfrac{2\pi}{B}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad B = \dfrac{2\pi}{\pi} = 2.]

The parameter [MATH: D] represents the vertical shift of the secant function. Since the local minimum of secant is [MATH: y=1,] we see that the function has been translated by [MATH: 2] units up. Therefore, [MATH: D=2.]

So, we have
[MATH: B+D = 2+2 = 4.]

Finally, the equation of the curve is

[MATH: y=\sec\left(2x\right)+2.]

Item 14 — Example: Identifying the Horizontal Shift of a Horizontally Stretched Secant or Cosecant Curve

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The parameter [MATH: C] represents a horizontal shift of the function.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring out the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

[MATH: y|= \sec (2x + C); = \sec (2(x + (C)/(2)))]

From the graph, we see that the graph of secant has been shifted by [MATH: \dfrac 1 2] units to the left. Therefore,

[MATH: \dfrac C 2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C = 1.]
